extracted.intended_audience: comics creators / cartoonists working with copy paper and print formats (mini-comics, floppy comics, photocopy production)
extracted.subtask_short: comic page layout with copy paper
extracted.subtask_description: Practical workbook for understanding and constructing comic-page proportions, grids, and live areas using common North American paper sizes (8.5x11, 11x17, etc.), with hands-on measuring/drawing exercises. Emphasizes how format, margins, and binding affect printed results and aesthetic 'feel'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand paper sizes and proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the common North American paper sizes (8.5 x 11, 11 x 17) and related comic dimensions (6 x 9 live area, 6.5 x 10.25 comic page, 9 x 12 double-page proportion) and how they relate proportionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece explains how 8.5 x 11 folded gives 5.5 x 8.5; 11 x 17 is proportionate to a 6 x 9 area; 6.5 x 10.25 floppy comic floats a 6 x 9 live area. Use the diagonal-line trick and direct measurement to compare proportions rather than assuming sizes will scale exactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and draw a correct live area
rubrics_metrics.description: Most North American comic books have a 'live area' (the containment lines that create margins) almost always 6 x 9 inches; the live area should be established and drawn within so artwork aligns to printed page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always mark and respect the live area on your originals; failure to do so leads to odd margins when printed (e.g., a digest with a wide top/bottom margin). The 6 x 9 live area typically floats on a 6.5 x 10.25-inch comic page.

rubrics_metrics.name: When drawing on 8.5 x 11, create a smaller internal drawing area
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume an 8.5 x 11 original will shrink exactly to digest proportions; instead create a specific inner area (the author suggests a 7 x 11 inch area) to draw within so the printed result lines up correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: drawing across full 8.5 x 11 expecting perfect scaling results in misaligned margins. Practical fix: measure and mark the appropriate internal rectangle before drawing so reduction preserves intended margins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the six-panel / 3x4 grid as a compositional standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard six-panel grid (three down, four across across a double-page spread) aligns with the 6 x 9 and 9 x 12 proportions and is a historically common compositional system for North American comics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a 9 x 12 area, divide into six squares on the 9-inch side and eight squares on the 12-inch side, then subdivide two squares per cell to produce two six-panel grids (one per page). The grid helps maintain consistent panel sizing and rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct harmonious proportions with geometric tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Use measuring, ruler, compass, and diagonal-line constructions (the 'diagonal line trick') to find centers, draw circles, and verify harmonic alignments in rectangles (e.g., 9 x 12) rather than relying on estimation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise: find center of 9 x 12 area, draw circle from center to east edge, draw diagonal 'bottom square' lines and their centers, then circles from those centers; observe that circles line up in the 9 x 12 proportion. Slightly different rectangles won't produce the same alignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work at a larger original scale (draw 'up') to allow margins and reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Create originals larger than the printed area (e.g., many North American originals at 10 x 15 inches, often described as 'drawn half up' / ~150%) so you can leave margins and reduce down for print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: drawing larger leaves a margin on the physical sheet (so the border isn't at the edge) and supports better reproduction when reduced. The page notes '10 x 15' is proportionate to 11 x 17 and is commonly used for original art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide between full-bleed and margined layouts and understand tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Be deliberate whether pages are full-bleed or contain margins: full-bleed removes margins for edge-to-edge imagery; margined pages preserve a framed live area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many modern comics go full-bleed, but the workbook focuses on margined pages. Consider printing limits, trimming, and how full-bleed affects panel composition and reproduction. The author limits discussion to margined examples for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for binding and format when designing spreads
rubrics_metrics.description: Binding type (stapled floppy vs perfect binding) affects whether a double-page spread can lay flat and thus whether the intended double-page proportion and 'harmony' will read correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 24-page floppy with staples lays flat and can realize the full 9 x 12 double-page harmony; perfect-bound books may not open flat and can constrain the center, altering the intended feel of a spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice concrete measuring/cutting/drawing exercises to internalize proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hands-on exercises—folding paper, marking 14 inches on 11 x 17 to make 11 x 14, cutting to leave a 9 x 12 area, measuring 1.5" margins, drawing grids, using colored pencils—help you internalize proportions and layout procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific steps provided: fold 8.5 x 11 to 5.5 x 8.5; place into corner of 11 x 17; measure 14" on 11x17 to create 11x14 then inset 1" to create 9x12; measure 1.5" along each side to create the grid; use colored pencil to draw panel lines so they are visible but separate from final inks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use visible but non-final marks for layout (colored pencils, containment lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark live areas, grid lines, and secondary construction lines in a different medium (e.g., colored pencil) so they are distinguishable from final inks and can guide composition without becoming part of the finished art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The workbook advises drawing a colored pencil line around the 9 x 12 area and using colored pencil to lay out vertical/horizontal panel lines; this clarifies construction vs final artwork and is a common studio practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let proportion guide creative decisions—proportion affects 'feel'
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that certain proportions (e.g., 9 x 12, 6 x 9) have a harmonic quality that influences how a comic 'feels' to readers; choose format and grid with aesthetic intent, not just convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the 9 x 12 proportion aligns circles and centers in a way the author finds 'remarkable'; some page sizes feel better when the book can lay flat. Consider these perceptual and tactile effects when planning format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize regional/commonalities in standard live areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard live areas for North American and European comics relate to the 9 x 12 proportion, so cross-regional formats can share harmonic properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: Tintin pages and North American live areas proportionally relate to 9 x 12, indicating shared compositional foundations across traditions; use this knowledge when choosing dimensions for international/translation work.
